items.title: The Christian Bible's contents were not fixed until centuries after Christ
items.claim: When was the New Testament canon — the 27 books — first listed in its current form?

options.text: By the apostles themselves, before 70 CE
At the Council of Nicaea in 325 CE
Athanasius's Easter letter of 367 CE is the first surviving list of exactly the 27 books; consensus formed gradually through the 4th-5th centuries
By Pope Damasus I at the Council of Trent in 1546

items.reveal:
Athanasius of Alexandria's 39th Festal Letter (367 CE) is the first surviving document listing the 27 NT books we have today. Regional councils (Hippo 393, Carthage 397) confirmed it. The Trent council (1546) made it formal Catholic dogma — partly in response to the Reformation.

Nicaea (325) dealt with the Arian controversy, not the canon — a common confusion popularised by Dan Brown's 'The Da Vinci Code'.

Gospels left out include Thomas, Mary, Peter and the Infancy Gospel of James. Some books that nearly made it (the Shepherd of Hermas, 1 Clement) didn't.
items.why: The 'received text' image of Scripture obscures a long, contested human process. Knowing the canon was assembled doesn't disprove faith — but it changes the questions you can ask.

items.title: The Hebrew Bible barely mentions an afterlife
items.claim: What does the Hebrew Bible (the Christian Old Testament) say about heaven and hell?

options.text: It describes both in detail throughout
It mostly speaks of Sheol — a shadowy underworld where the dead exist as shades — with explicit resurrection only in late texts like Daniel 12

items.reveal:
Job 3:13-19, Ecclesiastes 9:5-10 ('the dead know nothing') and the Psalms describe Sheol as a silent underworld common to all the dead. Daniel 12:2 (mid-2nd century BCE) is the clearest explicit resurrection passage — and it's one of the latest books.

By Jesus's time, Pharisees believed in resurrection and Sadducees did not (Mark 12:18-27). Christian heaven and hell as detailed afterlife destinations are largely shaped by intertestamental Jewish apocalyptic literature, Greek thought and later Christian elaboration (Dante most famously).
items.why: Students often assume the afterlife is a 'religious universal'. Within the Abrahamic tradition itself it's a developing idea, with the most familiar version being relatively recent.

items.title: Sikhism was founded by Guru Nanak in 1469
items.claim: Who founded Sikhism and what did he teach?

options.text: Guru Nanak (born 1469 at Nankana Sahib, in modern Pakistan) taught one God (Ek Onkar), equality of all people regardless of caste or gender, honest work (kirat karna), sharing with others (vand chakna), and remembrance of God (naam japna)

items.reveal_title: There is neither Hindu nor Muslim
items.reveal:
Born in 1469 at Nankana Sahib, Nanak had a transformative spiritual experience in 1499 — after emerging from three days at the Bein river he reportedly said 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim', pointing past religious labels to a shared underlying truth.

He undertook four major journeys (udasis) across India, into Tibet, the Middle East and possibly to Mecca. He died in 1539.

The Mool Mantar — Sikhism's foundational statement — begins 'Ik Onkar': there is one God. The Guru Granth Sahib opens with it.
items.why: Sikhism is the youngest of the major Indian religions — a deliberate rethinking of religious identity in Mughal-era Punjab. Its founding moment is well-attested historically, unlike older religions.
